questions.title: Beyond the AI summary
questions.prompt: You lead product at a project-management software company. Every competitor has added 'AI summaries'. The CEO asks where to invest in AI over the next 18 months. What is your strategy?
hints: Summaries are becoming a commodity. What do you have that a general-purpose assistant does not?
Which customer jobs in project management are slow, repetitive or error-prone?
How will falling model prices change the picture in 18 months?
followups: A general-purpose AI assistant can now read your customers' projects through an integration. Is that a threat or an opportunity?
Which bet would you kill first if early results are weak?
How do you price these features?
criteria: Starts from customer jobs, not from the technology.
Identifies a defensible advantage (workflow position, structured project data, permissions, distribution).
Sequences bets from assistive to more autonomous as trust grows.
Plans for commoditisation and integration with outside assistants.
Defines success metrics and kill criteria per bet.
outline: Jobs: status reporting, planning and estimation, risk spotting, intake triage, cross-project search.
Advantage: structured history of tasks, estimates, dates and outcomes; position in the daily workflow.
Bets: (1) automated status reports from real activity; (2) risk alerts from project history; (3) intake triage agent with approval.
Sequence: assist → automate with review → automate exceptions only.
Platform stance: expose data safely to outside assistants rather than block them.
Metrics: time saved per manager, adoption, accuracy of risk alerts, retention impact; kill criteria per bet.
questions.reference:
Summaries are table stakes, so I would not compete on them. Our advantage is the structured history of how projects actually run — tasks, estimates, slips, owners and outcomes — and our position in managers’ daily workflow. A general assistant can read a document; it does not know that this team’s estimates slip by 30%.

I would place three bets. First, status reports written from real activity, which saves managers time every week and is easy to check. Second, risk alerts: using project history to flag work likely to slip, which uses data competitors do not have. Third, an intake agent that turns requests into well-formed tasks and routes them, with human approval at first.

Each bet moves from assist to automate as accuracy is proven. I would also open our data to outside assistants through a permission-aware integration: if customers use them anyway, being the trusted source is better than being bypassed. Success is measured per bet — time saved, alert precision, adoption among active managers — with a review at six months where weak bets are cut. I would assume model costs keep falling, so I would not over-invest in our own models.
pitfalls: Another chatbot.
No view of what makes the bets defensible.
No kill criteria.

questions.title: Two answers and an invented policy
questions.prompt: A sales lead complains that your AI assistant gave two different answers to the same question, and once invented a refund policy that does not exist. Explain to them, in plain language, why this happens — and what you will change in the product.
hints: How does a language model choose its next word?
Where did the refund 'policy' come from if it is not in your documents?
Which product changes reduce each problem?
followups: Why not just set the temperature to zero?
Would fine-tuning on our policies fix the invented policy?
How would you tell customers the assistant can be wrong?
criteria: Explains next-token prediction and sampling without jargon.
Explains confabulation: fluent text without a grounding source.
Separates the two problems and their fixes.
Proposes grounding, citations, refusals and evaluation.
Sets honest expectations.
outline: Variation: the model picks likely words with some randomness; different wording or context changes the result.
Invention: the model produces plausible text; if no policy was retrieved, it can write a plausible one.
Fixes for consistency: lower randomness for factual answers, stable prompts, caching common answers.
Fixes for invention: retrieve the real policy, answer only from sources, cite them, refuse when nothing is found.
Measure: a test set of policy questions checked on every change.
questions.reference:
I would explain it like this: the assistant writes an answer one word at a time, choosing words that are likely given the question and the context it was given. There is some randomness in that choice, so the same question can produce two different answers — usually the same meaning in different words, but not always.

The invented refund policy is a different problem. The model is very good at writing text that sounds right. If it was not given our actual policy, it can write a plausible-sounding one. It is not lying; it has no way to know the difference unless we give it the source.

What we will change: for policy questions, the assistant will first look up the relevant policy page and answer only from it, with a link. If it cannot find a source, it will say so and offer to connect the customer to a person. We will reduce randomness for factual answers. And we will keep a test set of real policy questions that runs on every change, so we catch regressions before customers do. Turning randomness to zero helps consistency but does not stop invention; fine-tuning teaches style better than facts that change.
pitfalls: Saying the model 'knows' or 'looked it up'.
Promising it will never be wrong.

questions.title: An assistant for internal documents
questions.prompt: Employees at a 5,000-person company cannot find answers in thousands of internal documents. Design a retrieval-augmented (RAG) assistant: the main architecture choices, how permissions work, and how you would tell whether a bad answer came from retrieval or from generation.
hints: What happens if the assistant retrieves a document the user is not allowed to see?
Documents go out of date. How does the index stay fresh?
To separate retrieval failures from generation failures, what would you log?
followups: Answers are correct but users do not trust them. What do you add?
Why not just put all the documents into a very long context window?
HR asks to exclude certain documents entirely. How?
criteria: Describes the pipeline: ingestion, chunking, embeddings, retrieval, reranking, generation with citations.
Enforces permissions at retrieval time using the source system's access rules.
Plans freshness and deletion.
Evaluates retrieval (did the right passage come back?) separately from generation (was the answer faithful?).
Builds trust with citations and a clear 'I don't know'.
outline: Ingest from source systems with their access-control lists; re-index on change; honour deletions.
Chunk by document structure; embed; hybrid search (keyword + vector); rerank.
Filter results by the user's permissions before the model sees them.
Generate answers only from retrieved passages, with citations; refuse when retrieval is weak.
Log query, retrieved passages and answer; evaluate recall@k on a labelled set, and faithfulness of answers to passages.
Metrics: answer success rate, citation click-through, 'not helpful' rate, time saved.
questions.reference:
The pipeline: connect to source systems (wiki, drive, ticketing) and copy each document’s access rules along with its content; split documents by structure into passages; index them for both keyword and semantic search; rerank the top results; and have the model answer only from the retrieved passages, citing them.

Permissions are the critical design choice. Filtering must happen at retrieval, using the user’s identity, before any passage reaches the model — otherwise the model can quote a document the user should not see. Deletions and permission changes must propagate quickly, so the index syncs on change, not nightly.

To tell retrieval failures from generation failures, I would log the query, the passages retrieved and the answer. With a labelled set of real questions, I measure retrieval recall (was the right passage in the top results?) and, separately, faithfulness (does the answer say only what the passages say?). If the right passage was missing, fix retrieval — chunking, search, metadata; if it was present and the answer was wrong, fix the prompt or model.

A very long context window helps for a few documents but does not scale to thousands, costs more per question and still needs permission filtering.
pitfalls: Filtering permissions after generation.
One quality score for the whole pipeline.
Ignoring stale and deleted content.

questions.title: An expense-report agent
questions.prompt: Design an AI agent that handles employees' expense reports end to end: reading receipts, filling in the report, checking policy and submitting. What may it do on its own, and what needs a person?
hints: Which actions are reversible, and which move money?
What should happen when the receipt is unclear or the policy is ambiguous?
How could a malicious receipt or email try to manipulate the agent?
followups: Finance wants the agent to approve reports under a threshold automatically. What do you need first?
How do you measure whether the agent is good?
The agent occasionally loops, re-reading the same receipt. How do you detect and stop that?
criteria: Breaks the job into steps and tools with clear permissions.
Keeps irreversible or money-moving actions behind approval initially.
Designs for uncertainty: asks the employee, flags exceptions.
Addresses prompt injection from documents.
Measures task success, correction rate, policy violations, cost per report.
outline: Steps: extract receipt → categorise → check policy → draft report → employee confirms → submit → manager approves.
Autonomy: draft and check alone; submission needs employee confirmation; approval stays human until proven.
Uncertainty: low-confidence fields highlighted; policy ambiguity routed to the employee or finance.
Safety: treat receipt text as data, not instructions; limited tool permissions; spending limits.
Operations: step limits, loop detection, full audit trail.
Metrics: reports completed without correction, time saved, policy-violation rate, cost per report.
questions.reference:
I would split the job into steps — read the receipt, categorise, check policy, draft the report, submit, approve — and give the agent tools only for what each step needs.

At launch the agent may read, categorise, check and draft on its own, because those steps are reversible: the employee sees everything before it goes anywhere. Submission needs one click from the employee, and approval stays with the manager. Where the agent is unsure — a blurry total, an ambiguous policy — it highlights the field and asks rather than guessing.

Receipts and emails are untrusted input: text inside them is treated as data, never as instructions, and the agent cannot take actions outside its tools. Every action is logged for audit. Step limits and loop detection stop runaway behaviour.

I would measure reports completed without correction, time from receipt to submission, policy violations caught and missed, and cost per report. Automatic approval under a threshold comes only after months of data show the agent’s drafts match what managers approve, with random sampling continuing afterwards.
pitfalls: Full autonomy on day one.
Measuring steps taken instead of reports done right.
Ignoring prompt injection.

questions.title: Quality 'feels' worse
questions.prompt: Your team edits the assistant's system prompt almost every week. Support tickets suggest quality 'feels' worse than a month ago, but nobody can prove it. Set up an evaluation process.
hints: What would a fixed test set need to contain to be representative?
Who or what grades the answers, and how do you trust the grader?
How do you stop a fix for one problem breaking another?
followups: You use a model to grade answers. How do you know it grades like a person would?
Your golden set is six months old. Is it still valid?
How do you decide whether a change is good enough to ship?
criteria: Builds a versioned golden set from real traffic covering important intents and hard cases.
Defines graders and calibrates model graders against human labels.
Compares every change against the current baseline before shipping.
Tracks regressions per segment, not only an average.
Refreshes the set from production failures.
outline: Collect: sample real conversations by intent; add known failures and edge cases; label expected properties.
Grade: automatic checks (format, citations), rubric-based human review, model graders calibrated on human labels.
Process: every prompt or model change runs the suite; results compared with baseline per segment.
Ship rule: no regression beyond threshold on critical intents; overall improvement.
Maintain: weekly sample of production failures added to the set; quarterly refresh.
questions.reference:
First, a golden set: a few hundred real conversations sampled by intent, plus every known failure, each labelled with what a good answer must do (cite the policy, refuse a medical question, ask for an order number). The set is versioned like code.

Second, graders. Simple properties get automatic checks. Quality judgments use a written rubric, scored by people on a sample and by a model grader on the full set. I would check the model grader against human labels and only trust it where they agree well.

Third, process. No prompt or model change ships without running the suite and comparing to the current baseline, broken down by intent — an average can hide a large drop in one important area. The ship rule is written in advance: no critical intent regresses beyond a threshold.

Finally, keep it honest: each week, add a sample of real production failures to the set. To answer the ‘feels worse’ question now, I would run last month’s prompt and this week’s prompt on the new set side by side.
pitfalls: Demos instead of a test set.
Trusting a model grader without calibration.
One average score.

questions.title: Hosted or open-weight for contract review
questions.prompt: You are building a contract-review feature for law firms in the EU. Choose between a proprietary frontier model through an API and an open-weight model you host yourself.
hints: What do law firms require about where client data goes?
How would you compare quality on this task specifically?
What does running your own model cost beyond the hardware?
followups: The proprietary model scores clearly higher on your evaluation. Does that settle it?
How do you avoid being locked into either choice?
A cheaper model appears in six months. What is your process?
criteria: Lists requirements: quality on legal text, data residency and confidentiality, latency, cost, customisation.
Evaluates on a task-specific set, not public benchmarks.
Weighs operational costs and team skills of self-hosting.
Considers hybrid and contractual options (regional hosting, no-training terms).
Designs for switching.
outline: Requirements: accuracy on clause extraction and risk flags; confidentiality; EU data residency; audit; cost per contract.
Evaluate candidates on a labelled set of real (anonymised, permitted) contracts.
Proprietary API: higher capability, faster to ship; check regional hosting and contractual data terms.
Open-weight: control, on-premises option for strict clients, cost at scale; needs serving and safety work.
Decision and hybrid option; abstraction layer and portable evals; quarterly re-evaluation.
questions.reference:
I would start with requirements, because law firms will decide on confidentiality before quality: client documents must stay in approved regions, must not be used for training, and access must be auditable. Then quality on our task — finding clauses and flagging risk accurately — then latency and cost per contract.

I would test both options on a labelled set of real contracts we have permission to use, not on public benchmarks. If the proprietary model is clearly more accurate and the provider offers EU hosting with contractual no-training and retention terms, it is the faster route to a good product. If some clients require on-premises deployment, an open-weight model may be the only option for them, at the cost of our own serving, monitoring and safety work.

A likely answer is hybrid: the hosted model by default, an open-weight deployment for the strictest clients. Either way I would keep an abstraction layer and a portable evaluation set, so switching models is a test run, not a rewrite — and re-evaluate when new models arrive.
pitfalls: Choosing by leaderboard.
Ignoring confidentiality requirements.
Underestimating self-hosting effort.

questions.title: The support assistant MVP
questions.prompt: You are launching a GenAI-powered customer support assistant. How would you design the MVP, choose success metrics, evaluate hallucination risks, and decide whether the product is ready for production?
hints: Which customer questions are safe to automate first, and which are not?
What does success mean for the customer, the support team and the business?
What is your launch bar, and who can stop the launch?
followups: Resolution rate is high but customer satisfaction dropped. What happened?
The assistant must never promise a refund it cannot give. How do you enforce that?
Agents fear for their jobs. How does that affect your rollout?
criteria: Scopes the MVP to a few high-volume, low-risk intents with a fast path to a person.
Grounds answers in approved help content and account data, with citations.
Defines success across customer, team and business, with guardrails.
Evaluates hallucination risk before launch with a test set and red-teaming.
Sets explicit launch criteria and a staged rollout with rollback.
outline: MVP: top 5–10 intents (order status, password reset, shipping policy); everything else goes to a person.
Design: retrieval from approved content; account lookups through tools; citations; easy handoff with context.
Hard rules: never commit refunds, legal statements or account changes without a person.
Metrics: resolution without contact (primary), customer satisfaction, repeat contact within 7 days, escalation quality, cost per resolution; guardrails on complaints and wrong-answer reports.
Evaluation: labelled set by intent; faithfulness checks; adversarial tests (refund pressure, injection).
Launch bar: thresholds per intent; staged rollout 5% → 25% → 100%; kill switch; weekly review.
questions.reference:
MVP scope: the five to ten most common, low-risk questions — order status, password resets, shipping and returns policy — where answers come from approved content or a read-only account lookup. Everything else, and anything the customer asks for, goes to a person, with the conversation passed along so they never repeat themselves.

The assistant answers only from retrieved help content and account data, and shows its source. Some things it may never do: promise refunds, make legal statements or change accounts. Those are enforced in code and tools, not only in the prompt.

Success has three sides. For customers: resolved without needing to contact us again within seven days, and satisfaction. For the support team: fewer repetitive tickets and better handoffs. For the business: cost per resolution. Guardrails: complaints, wrong-answer reports and escalation rate.

Before launch: a labelled test set per intent, measured for correctness and faithfulness to sources, plus adversarial tests — customers pressing for refunds, attempts to override instructions. The launch bar is written down per intent; intents that fail stay with people. Rollout is staged with a kill switch, and a named owner can stop it. ‘High resolution, lower satisfaction’ usually means the assistant is ending conversations without solving them — that is why repeat contact is the primary measure, not deflection.
pitfalls: Measuring deflection instead of resolution.
Relying on the prompt alone to stop risky commitments.
No written launch bar.

questions.title: Explaining insurance decisions
questions.prompt: A health insurer wants an AI assistant that explains claim decisions to its members in plain language. Identify the main harms and set a launch bar.
hints: Who could be hurt, and how badly, if the explanation is wrong?
What personal and health data does the assistant touch?
Should the assistant ever give an opinion on whether the decision was right?
followups: A member asks the assistant whether they should appeal. What does it say?
How do you test that explanations are faithful to the actual decision?
Regulators ask how you prevent unfair outcomes. What do you show them?
criteria: Lists harms by severity: wrong explanation, discouraging valid appeals, privacy leaks, unequal quality across groups, misuse.
Grounds explanations in the actual decision record and policy text.
Keeps the assistant from deciding or advising on appeals; always shows the appeal route.
Protects health data: minimisation, access control, no training without consent.
Defines a measurable launch bar with an owner who can stop it.
outline: Harms: incorrect or misleading explanations; members not appealing valid claims; disclosure of health data; lower quality for some languages or groups; manipulation attempts.
Design: generate only from the claim record and cited policy clauses; plain-language templates for common denial reasons.
Boundaries: explains, never judges; always shows appeal rights and a human contact.
Privacy: verified identity; least data; retention limits; no training on member data without consent.
Testing: faithfulness checks against records; red-team; quality by language and demographic proxies.
Launch bar: faithfulness above threshold on every denial type; zero privacy leaks in testing; human review sample; owner and kill switch.
questions.reference:
The worst harm is a wrong or misleading explanation that leads a member not to appeal a claim they would have won. Others: exposing health information to the wrong person, giving worse explanations in some languages, and people trying to manipulate the assistant into ‘approving’ something.

So the assistant explains, and never judges. It writes only from the actual claim record and the policy clauses cited in the decision, shows those sources, and always ends with the member’s appeal rights and how to reach a person. Asked ‘should I appeal?’, it explains the process and deadlines and offers a human — it does not advise.

Privacy: identity verification before any claim detail, the minimum data per answer, short retention, no training on member data without explicit consent.

Launch bar, written before testing: explanations are faithful to the record in at least an agreed share of cases for every denial type, with zero cases that misstate appeal rights; no data leaks in red-team testing; comparable quality across supported languages. A named owner — not the project team alone — signs off and can stop the launch, and a sample of live conversations is reviewed by people every week.
pitfalls: Treating safety as a filter on the output.
Letting the assistant advise on appeals.
A launch bar with no numbers or owner.

questions.title: An AI feature that loses money
questions.prompt: Your AI writing feature costs $0.12 per use in model calls. Active users use it 40 times a month, and they pay $10 a month. Fix the economics without making the product worse.
questions.premise: All figures are invented for practice.
hints: What share of revenue goes to model calls today?
Are all uses equally hard? Could a smaller model handle most of them?
What is the cost of a use that needs a retry?
followups: The smaller model is slightly worse on long documents. How do you route?
Usage doubles next quarter. What breaks?
Would you change the pricing?
criteria: Computes the current unit economics.
Measures cost per successful task, including retries.
Proposes routing, caching, context trimming and output limits.
Protects quality with evaluation per route.
Considers pricing and limits for heavy users.
outline: Unit economics: cost per user per month vs price.
Breakdown: tokens in vs out; context size; retries; distribution of task difficulty.
Levers: route simple tasks to a smaller model; trim context; cache repeated prompts; cap output length; stream for perceived latency.
Guard quality: evaluate each route; send hard cases to the large model.
Pricing: usage tiers or fair-use limits for heavy users.
Target margin and monitoring.
questions.reference:
Today an active user costs $4.80 a month in model calls on a $10 plan — 48% of revenue before any other cost. That is not sustainable.

First I would measure where the cost comes from: input versus output tokens, how much context we send, how often users retry, and how difficulty varies. Usually a large share of requests are simple — rephrasing a sentence — and a small share are hard, such as rewriting a long document.

Levers, in order: route simple requests to a smaller, cheaper model and keep the large model for hard ones; send only the relevant part of the document instead of all of it; cache repeated system prompts; cap output length where users rarely need more. Each route is checked against the evaluation set so quality holds where users notice it.

If heavy users still cost more than they pay, I would introduce a fair-use limit or a higher tier rather than degrading everyone’s experience. I would track cost per successful task — not per call — because a cheap model that needs three retries is not cheap.
pitfalls: Cutting cost by using a worse model everywhere.
Measuring cost per call, not per completed task.

questions.title: Reviewing AI-drafted complaint replies
questions.prompt: A bank wants an AI to draft replies to customer complaints, reviewed by staff before sending. Design the human review step so that it is a real control, not a rubber stamp.
hints: What does a reviewer need to see to check a draft in under a minute?
How would you know reviewers are approving without reading?
When could review be reduced, and on what evidence?
followups: Reviewers approve 99% of drafts. Is that good news?
How do reviewer corrections improve the system?
Which complaints should never be drafted by AI?
criteria: Places review where errors are costly (regulated responses, compensation).
Designs the review screen: sources, highlighted claims, risk flags, diff from templates.
Detects rubber-stamping (seeded errors, time-on-task, agreement audits).
Uses corrections as training and evaluation data.
Defines evidence needed before reducing review.
outline: Scope: complaints by type; exclude vulnerable-customer and legal-threat cases from AI drafting.
Screen: draft beside complaint and account facts; claims linked to sources; regulatory phrases checked; changes tracked.
Controls: seeded test drafts with known errors; second review of a sample; time-on-task monitoring.
Learning: every edit labelled (fact, tone, policy) and added to evaluation.
Path: reduce review only for complaint types with sustained low error rates, with continued sampling.
questions.reference:
Review is only a control if reviewers can check quickly and are actually checking. I would exclude some complaints from AI drafting entirely: vulnerable customers, legal threats and fraud claims go straight to specialists.

For the rest, the review screen shows the complaint, the account facts the draft relies on and the draft side by side, with each factual claim linked to its source and regulated wording checked automatically. Anything the system is unsure about is highlighted. Reviewers edit inline, and every edit is labelled — fact, tone, policy — which feeds the evaluation set.

To detect rubber-stamping, I would seed occasional drafts with known errors and measure how many are caught, audit a sample with a second reviewer, and watch time spent per draft. A 99% approval rate is only good news if the seeded errors are caught.

Review can be reduced for a complaint type only after sustained evidence of low error rates, with random sampling continuing and an automatic return to full review if errors rise.
pitfalls: Reviewers with no sources on screen.
Celebrating high approval rates.
No path to reduce or restore review.

questions.title: Pricing AI meeting notes
questions.prompt: Your video-conferencing product is adding AI meeting notes and action items. How would you package and price it, and how would you prove ROI to business buyers?
hints: Who pays — the individual user or the company — and what do they value?
What does each meeting cost you to process?
Competitors may bundle similar features for free. How does that affect you?
followups: A competitor includes it free in every plan. Respond.
Finance asks for the gross margin at 3× usage. What do you need to know?
How do you measure 'time saved' credibly?
criteria: Identifies buyer and value metric.
Compares packaging options (bundle, add-on seat, usage) with pros and cons.
Checks margin with realistic usage and costs.
Plans ROI proof with a baseline or holdout.
Anticipates competitive bundling.
outline: Value: time saved writing notes, fewer missed follow-ups, searchable decisions.
Options: bundle into premium tier; per-seat add-on; usage-based minutes.
Margin: processing cost per meeting hour × hours per seat vs price.
Choice: per-seat add-on for business plans, limited free tier to drive adoption.
ROI: compare teams with and without; measure follow-up completion and note-taking time.
Competitive response: differentiate on accuracy, integrations, privacy controls.
questions.reference:
The buyer is the company; the value is time saved and follow-ups that actually happen. I would price a per-seat add-on on business plans — easy for buyers to budget — with a small free allowance on every plan so people experience it.

Before setting the price, I would compute margin: processing cost per meeting hour × typical meeting hours per seat, at today’s usage and at three times today’s, against the add-on price. If heavy users would be unprofitable, include a generous fair-use limit.

For ROI, I would offer pilots with a comparison: teams using the feature versus similar teams without it, measuring time spent writing notes (survey plus calendar data), action-item completion and meetings needed to revisit decisions. A buyer believes a before-and-after from their own teams more than a vendor’s average.

If a competitor makes it free, I would not race to zero; I would compete on accuracy, integrations with the buyer’s task tools and privacy controls — and consider bundling into a higher tier if the add-on is not winning.
pitfalls: Pricing without knowing cost per meeting.
ROI claims without a comparison group.

questions.title: Better offline, worse in production
questions.prompt: You own the fraud model for a payments app. The new model scored better than the old one offline, but chargebacks have risen since it shipped. Investigate.
hints: How long does it take to learn that a payment was fraud?
Was the offline test set like today's traffic?
Could the old model have shaped the data the new one learned from?
followups: Rolling back costs a week of engineering work. Do it anyway?
How would you test the next model before full launch?
Which metric should the fraud team be measured on?
criteria: Recognises label delay: chargebacks arrive weeks later.
Checks for distribution shift and data or feature bugs.
Identifies feedback loops (blocked transactions have no labels).
Compares models online with a holdout or shadow mode.
Ties model metrics to business outcome: fraud loss vs false declines.
outline: Confirm: chargebacks by transaction date vs report date; compare cohorts.
Check pipeline: feature differences between training and serving; missing features.
Shift: new merchants, regions or fraud patterns not in the test set.
Feedback loop: old model's blocks removed labels for some fraud types.
Action: limit exposure (rollback or raise threshold); run shadow or holdout comparison.
Metrics: fraud loss + cost of false declines; launch rule for next model.
questions.reference:
First, check the chargeback rise is about the new model: chargebacks arrive weeks after the payment, so I would compare by transaction date and see whether payments scored by the new model have higher fraud rates than similar payments scored by the old one.

Then the usual causes. A training–serving difference: a feature computed differently in production, or missing. A shift: new merchants, regions or a new fraud pattern absent from the offline test set. And a feedback loop: transactions the old model blocked never produced labels, so the new model learned less about exactly the fraud the old model was catching.

While investigating, I would limit losses — roll back or raise the threshold — because fraud losses are real money. The next model should run in shadow mode or against a holdout before full launch, evaluated on fraud loss plus the cost of false declines (good customers blocked), not only offline precision. I would also keep a small random sample of transactions approved with lower scrutiny, so we still learn what we would otherwise block.
pitfalls: Trusting offline metrics as the answer.
Forgetting label delay.
Ignoring false declines.

questions.title: Research says no, sales said yes
questions.prompt: Your sales team told a large customer that a new AI feature would be ready next month. The research team says the model does not yet meet the quality bar, and it may take another quarter. You are in the middle. What do you do?
hints: What exactly is below the bar, and for which use cases?
Is there a smaller version that is good enough?
Who should talk to the customer, and with what message?
followups: The customer threatens to cancel. Does that change the quality bar?
Research cannot give a date. How do you plan?
How do you stop sales over-promising AI features in future?
criteria: Understands the quality gap specifically.
Looks for a scoped launch that meets the bar.
Protects the quality bar; does not trade safety for a deal.
Communicates honestly with the customer, with a plan.
Fixes the process for future commitments.
outline: Clarify the gap with research: which tasks fail, how often, how badly.
Options: scoped launch for the use cases that pass; preview with clear limits; wait.
Customer conversation with sales: what is ready, when, with what evidence.
Hold the bar; escalate if pressure continues.
Process: AI features committed only after passing evaluation; sales enablement on limits.
questions.reference:
I would first get specific with research: which tasks fall below the bar, how often and how badly. Often the model is good enough for some use cases and not others.

If so, I would propose a scoped launch next month for the use cases that pass, with the rest as a clearly labelled preview or a later release. If nothing passes, we wait — I would not lower the quality bar to save a deal, because a visible failure at a large customer costs more than a delay.

I would join sales in talking to the customer: what is ready, what is not, why, and what evidence will tell us when it is. Customers usually accept an honest plan better than a broken feature.

Afterwards, I would change the process: AI features are committed to customers only after they pass evaluation, and sales gets a short guide to what the feature can and cannot do.
pitfalls: Lowering the bar under pressure.
Letting sales manage the customer alone.
No process change.

questions.title: An AI launch that disappointed
questions.prompt: Tell me about an AI or machine-learning feature you worked on whose quality in production was worse than expected. How did you find out, and what did you do?
hints: Be specific about the gap between testing and production.
What signal told you, and how quickly?
What did you change in how the team evaluates?
followups: What would have caught it before launch?
How did you communicate it to users or customers?
What would you do differently?
criteria: Specific example with real consequences.
Explains why testing missed it.
Acted quickly: mitigation, communication.
Improved evaluation or monitoring afterwards.
Owns the outcome.
outline: Context and the feature.
What testing showed and what production showed.
How the gap was detected.
Immediate actions.
Root cause and lasting fix to evaluation.
Lessons.
questions.reference: A strong answer (a model of structure, not a script): “Our search ranking model beat the old one in offline tests, but after launch, searches with zero clicks rose for long queries. We found out from a weekly dashboard by query length. Our test set had very few long queries because it was sampled by volume. We rolled back for long queries within a day, rebuilt the test set stratified by query type, and relaunched two weeks later with a guardrail on zero-click rate by segment. Since then every model launch is reviewed segment by segment, not only on the overall metric.”
pitfalls: Blaming the data science team.
No change to evaluation afterwards.
